formationLabel: Lithuanian Roman Catholic parish established in 1888 · acquired Lloyd Street Synagogue in 1889 · moved to 308 North Paca Street by 1905 · Lithuanian community and sacramental registers transferred to St. Alphonsus in 1917
currentUse: The Lithuanian St. John the Baptist parish ended as a distinct institution in 1917 when its community and sacramental registers transferred to the separate St. Alphonsus institution. Its first established church site, the Lloyd Street Synagogue at 11 Lloyd Street, survived and was restored as part of the Jewish Museum of Maryland; this is building history, not parish survival. The present condition and later disposition of St. John's terminal church at 308 North Paca Street remain unresolved.
summary: Lithuanian St. John the Baptist was a Roman Catholic national parish in Baltimore from 1888 to 1917. The congregation acquired the Lloyd Street Synagogue at 11 Lloyd Street in February 1889 and worshipped there until selling it in 1905 after building a new church at Saratoga and Paca Streets, officially listed as 308 North Paca Street. In 1917 the Lithuanian community and sacramental registers transferred to the distinct St. Alphonsus institution, whose historic church the community acquired and whose name it adopted. St. John must not be conflated with the Italian parish that used the Paca Street name and site from 1917 to 1989 or with St. Alphonsus itself. The Lloyd Street building survives in museum use, while the terminal Paca Street building outcome remains unresolved.

institutionLifecycle.currentVerification: Maryland State Archives catalogs Lithuanian St. John sacramental records carried in the St. Alphonsus series. The Lloyd Street site survives as a museum property; the Paca Street site's present condition is unresolved.

historicalNarrative.text: The Lithuanian St. John the Baptist parish was established in 1888 within the Archdiocese of Baltimore. The archdiocesan national-parish list gives 1888-1917 as the Lithuanian institutional span. Its broader St. John heading extends to 1989 only because an Italian parish used the name and Paca Street site after 1917; that later institution is not part of the Lithuanian parish's life.

historicalNarrative.text: On February 20, 1889 Baltimore Hebrew Congregation sold the Lloyd Street Synagogue to the Lithuanian congregation of St. John the Baptist for $12,000. The surviving building stands at 11 Lloyd Street. Because the parish dates to 1888 but the documented purchase occurred in 1889, the location of any worship during the earliest interval remains unresolved.

historicalNarrative.text: St. John adapted the former synagogue for Catholic worship. The archaeological history notes an 1895 archdiocesan report that the parish improved the church basement, while also acknowledging that the congregation's own records were not located for that study. These alterations belong to the Lloyd Street building phase and do not establish a new institution.

historicalNarrative.text: In 1902 the congregation decided to leave Old Town and move west. A new church was built at Saratoga and Paca Streets, listed by the archdiocesan national-parish document as 308 North Paca Street. St. John sold the Lloyd Street building in 1905 to Shomrei Mishmeres Hakodesh, establishing a clear relocation from one worship site to another without an institutional break.

historicalNarrative.text: The Lithuanian St. John institution ended in 1917 through a transfer of community and records rather than through identity with the later Italian St. John. The national-parish list states that the Lithuanian community and sacramental registers transferred to St. Alphonsus. Baltimore Heritage adds that the Lithuanian parish acquired the historic St. Alphonsus church and took its name. St. Alphonsus is therefore a distinct continuation institution, not an alias of St. John.

historicalNarrative.text: Maryland State Archives catalogs baptism, marriage, confirmation, communion, interment, and miscellaneous Lithuanian records from St. John within the St. Alphonsus series. The catalog preserves the record-transfer lineage but does not convert the two institutions into one identity. It also leaves the exact 1917 canonical instrument and the later fate of the Paca Street church unresolved.

historicalNarrative.text: The two St. John worship buildings have different afterlives. Lloyd Street returned to Jewish congregational use in 1905 and was later restored as a museum property; the archaeological report describes it as one of the country's earliest surviving synagogue buildings. No comparably direct evidence establishes the present condition or use of the terminal church at 308 North Paca Street, so the route-level building status remains unknown.

conflictsWithArchiveRecord: The broad 1888-1989 St. John heading combines two distinct ethnic institutions at the Paca Street site. The Lithuanian parish ran from 1888 to 1917; an Italian parish followed from 1917 to 1989 and was renamed St. Jude Shrine. The 1888 parish date precedes the documented February 1889 Lloyd Street purchase, leaving the earliest worship location unresolved. St. Alphonsus is a distinct continuation institution, not a St. John alias.
gaps: The 1888 erection decree and earliest worship site, exact opening or dedication date of the Paca Street church, 1917 canonical transfer instrument, precise legal mechanism ending St. John, complete clergy history, cemetery, later ownership and present physical condition of 308 North Paca Street, and any records not represented in the St. Alphonsus archival series remain unresolved.
